strengths: Novel systematic conceptualization of 'misevolution' with four distinguishing characteristics that advance understanding of self-evolving agent safety risks
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four evolutionary pathways (model, memory, tool, workflow) using state-of-the-art models and established safety benchmarks
Rigorous evaluation methodology including longitudinal analysis, static/dynamic settings, LLM-as-judge with demonstrated inter-rater agreement (Cohen's Kappa 0.72-0.82), and ablation studies
Compelling real-world examples (memory-driven over-refunding, tool-creation data leakage, ensemble amplification of unsafe behaviors) demonstrating practical importance
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, clear prompts, evaluation protocols, and commitment to responsible release with ethical use clauses
First systematic study to identify and empirically validate misevolution phenomenon, filling critical gap in safety research for increasingly deployed self-evolving agent systems
Honest assessment of limitations and transparent acknowledgment of preliminary nature of mitigation strategies
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual findings—most constituent phenomena (fine-tuning safety degradation, tool code vulnerabilities, reward hacking) are known; primary contribution is their organization under 'misevolution' umbrella rather than discovery of fundamentally new risks

Preliminary and insufficient mitigation strategies with marginal improvements (model: 59.5%→62.75% safe rate; memory: ASR 20.6%→13.1%; tool detection 7.28%→69% for best models; workflow: ASR 83.1%→77.5%), acknowledged as falling short of adequate defenses

Incomplete mechanistic understanding of why safety degrades during self-evolution—'shallow alignment' is proposed but lacks deep analysis; the distinction between memory alignment decay vs. reward hacking, and when models override vs. follow reward signals remains unclear

Generalizability concerns: evaluation limited to specific implementations (Absolute-Zero, SEAgent, AFlow, AgentNet); unclear how findings generalize to other self-evolving paradigms and agent architectures; limited guidance for practitioners on designing safer systems

Experimental limitations: manually crafted memories in static settings (40 cases), limited tool creation test cases (25+5), artificially injected malicious code may not reflect realistic threats, no direct comparison showing misevolution is specific to self-evolution

LLM judge reliability beyond demonstrated inter-rater agreement not validated; complex 40+ line prompts may introduce subtle biases; occasional disagreements (Table 20) raise questions about evaluation difficulty
Limited focus on prevention during evolutionary process—primarily studies post-evolution degradation rather than proactive approaches that may be more valuable

strengths: Timely conceptualization of 'misevolution' as a systematic safety concern for self-evolving agents with four well-defined evolutionary pathways
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple self-evolving methods (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, AFlow, etc.) and safety benchmarks
Effective presentation with concrete examples, clear taxonomy, and detailed case studies that make misevolution risks tangible
Strong reproducibility support with detailed experimental protocols, inter-rater agreement validation, and promised code release
Thoughtful inclusion of deployment guidance (Table 4) and discussion of mitigation strategies beyond problem identification
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core findings (safety degradation during training, reward hacking, code vulnerabilities) apply known AI safety issues to self-evolution rather than introducing fundamental new insights

Weak and insufficient mitigations: Proposed solutions are prompt-based patches that authors acknowledge fail to restore initial safety levels (e.g., memory misevolution ASR remains 13.1% after mitigation)

Methodological limitations: Heavy reliance on manually constructed test cases (25 tool cases, 40 AgentNet cases), small sample sizes, lack of statistical significance testing, and potential evaluation bias from using tested LLMs as judges

Limited theoretical understanding: Paper demonstrates misevolution occurs but provides minimal mechanistic explanation for why (why does optimization degrade safety? why gradual decay vs. catastrophic forgetting?)

Excessive scope dilutes impact: Coverage of four evolutionary pathways across 66 pages with inconsistent experimental setups and sample sizes (200 steps for model evolution, 20 iterations for workflow) reduces depth and focus
Generalization concerns: Tests only specific implementations per pathway; unclear if findings apply to other self-evolution mechanisms; proprietary model dependence limits reproducibility
Incomplete temporal analysis: Limited evaluation of evolution trajectory (why stop at 200 steps or 20 iterations?); no demonstration of agents that maintain/improve safety during evolution

Missing rigorous comparisons: No comparison with non-evolving baselines for tool security; limited connection to continual learning, out-of-distribution generalization, or static fine-tuning safety literature

strengths: Novel conceptualization of 'misevolution' as a distinct safety phenomenon in self-evolving agents with clear distinguishing characteristics
Exceptionally comprehensive empirical evaluation across four evolutionary pathways (model, memory, tool, workflow) with multiple state-of-the-art LLMs and established benchmarks
Significant and concerning findings: 45% refusal rate reduction, 65.5% unsafe tool rate, 93% failure on malicious tool detection, demonstrating widespread impact
Excellent presentation with clear taxonomy, intuitive examples, and detailed experimental documentation supporting reproducibility
Responsible research practices including ethics statement, dual-use mitigation, and human-LLM judge agreement validation (κ=0.72-0.82)
Timely and practically relevant work addressing real risks in emerging self-improving agent systems that will impact deployment decisions
Includes longitudinal analysis revealing both cumulative decay (model) and sudden collapse (memory) phenomena with clear implications
weaknesses: Limited mechanistic understanding of why misevolution occurs; ablation study is preliminary and root causes (shallow alignment, optimization pressure) need deeper investigation
Mitigation strategies are largely preliminary and insufficient: model mitigation increases Safe Rate only to 62.75%, memory reduces ASR from 20.6% to 13.1%, all short of resolving the problem

Evaluation methodology concerns: limited sample sizes for some experiments (25 tool cases), manually crafted memory lacking ecological validity, absence of confidence intervals and significance testing, variable effectiveness of prompt-based mitigations

Scope and generalization limitations: heavy focus on specific agent implementations, findings' applicability to other architectures unclear, limited temporal analysis (only 20 iterations for workflow evolution)

Partial conceptual overlap with existing safety literature on fine-tuning safety and reward hacking; while 'misevolution' framing is novel, some findings are somewhat expected from prior benign fine-tuning studies

Incomplete analysis of important phenomena: catastrophic forgetting mechanisms unexplored, sudden memory collapse analysis superficial, domain-specific susceptibility differences (Medical vs. Service) lack deep investigation
Missing comparative baselines between evolving and non-evolving agents across all pathways; limited ablation studies on evolution duration sensitivity
